# Lawmakers advance AI transparency bill

The state senate voted 31–8 on Tuesday to advance a bill requiring companies that deploy AI assistants in customer service to disclose when a customer is talking to a machine.

The bill would also require providers of large language models above a certain size to publish summaries of their safety testing, including red-teaming results and how they handle prompt injection and jailbreak attempts.

"People deserve to know whether the agent on the other end is a person or a model," said the bill's sponsor. Industry groups argued the testing disclosures could hand attackers a roadmap, and asked for a delay of two years.

Consumer advocates welcomed the vote but said the bill does not go far enough. They want a private right of action when an AI assistant gives harmful financial or medical advice.

The bill now goes to the house, where a companion measure has stalled in committee. If it passes, the disclosure rules would take effect next July.

Several large employers in the state already label automated chat. A spokesperson for one retailer said its assistant introduces itself as "a virtual assistant" in the first message and hands off to a human on request.

Analysts expect similar bills in at least a dozen states next year, and some companies say they would rather follow one national standard than a patchwork of state rules.
